sections.text:
Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable.

We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities.

Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels.

On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

summary.en: RoboACE jointly evolves a curriculum and an execution harness around frozen foundation models. The curriculum proposes challenges using accumulated capability evidence, while the execution harness makes reusable revisions to expand capabilities. Alternating updates keep one side fixed while the other changes, and fixed challenge snapshots support comparisons. The authors report that a frozen deployment, initialized from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, outperforms evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO it achieves 74.0% success, 15.0 percentage points above the initial deployment. Case studies describe changes in practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are effective as end-to-end motion planners, but can be brittle when evaluated in closed-loop settings due to being trained under traditional imitation learning framework. Existing closed-loop supervision approaches lack scalability and fail to completely model a reactive environment.

We propose MAPLE, a novel framework for reactive, multi-agent rollout of a dynamic driving scenario in the latent space of the VLA model. The ego vehicle and nearby traffic agents are independently controlled over multi-step horizons, while being reactive to other agents in the scene, enabling closed-loop training.

MAPLE consists of two training stages: （1） supervised fine-tuning on the latent rollouts based on ground-truth trajectories, followed by （2） reinforcement learning with global and agent -specific rewards that encourage safety, progress, and interaction realism.

We further propose diversity rewards that encourage the model to generate planning behaviors that may not be present in logged driving data. Notably, our closed-loop training framework is scalable and does not require external simulators, which can be computationally expensive to run and have limited visual fidelity to the real-world.

MAPLE achieves state-of-the-art driving performance on Bench2Drive and demonstrates scalable, closed-loop multi-agent play for robust E2E autonomous driving systems.

summary.en: MAPLE performs reactive multi-agent rollouts of dynamic driving scenes in a vision-language-action model's latent space. The ego vehicle and nearby traffic agents are independently controlled over multi-step horizons and respond to one another, supporting closed-loop training. Training has two stages: supervised fine-tuning on latent rollouts derived from ground-truth trajectories, followed by reinforcement learning with global and agent-specific rewards for safety, progress, and interaction realism. Diversity rewards encourage behaviors that may be absent from logged data. The authors describe the framework as scalable and simulator-free and report state-of-the-art driving performance on Bench2Drive.

items.title: MAPLE: Latent Multi-Agent Play for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

sections.text:
Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model.

We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making.

To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes.

Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted.

For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.

Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality.

The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.

summary.en: GEMOR-GS targets LiDAR-inertial-visual SLAM with a geometrically accurate, globally refined, re-enterable 3D Gaussian map. It estimates LiDAR-camera extrinsics offline on dedicated calibration segments, alternately refines keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters, then rebuilds the global reconstruction from refined keyframes. After tracking loss, relocalization uses an XFeat bypass map, coarse RANSAC-PnP localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences report reconstruction and relocalization results, with held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The authors conclude the method improves map geometry, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability.
summary.zh: GEMOR-GS面向激光雷达、惯性与视觉SLAM，旨在生成几何准确、全局优化且可重新进入的3D高斯地图。方法先在专用标定片段上离线估计激光雷达与相机外参，再交替优化关键帧位姿和高斯参数，并从优化后的关键帧重建全局地图。跟踪丢失后，通过绕行地图、RANSAC-PnP粗定位及高斯RGB-D变形细化恢复位姿。在一组自采和五组公开序列上的实验报告了重建质量与重定位结果，并指出重定位成功率与外参质量有关。

sections.text:
Many rehabilitation robots execute prescribed motions using reactive tracking controllers that do not explicitly incorporate the user's instantaneous human-ground interaction. This paper presents Ground Reaction Force-Aware Model Predictive Control (GRF-MPC), a framework for upright physical assistance.

By integrating live GRF and center of pressure (CoP) measurements directly into a human centroidal dynamics model, GRF-MPC formulates a real-time quadratic program (QP) that optimizes assistive forces and moments over a receding horizon.

We deployed GRF-MPC on the Robotic Upright Stand Trainer (RobUST) in an underactuated 4-cable configuration and evaluated it against a fully actuated 8-cable Cartesian impedance baseline in nearly 300 trials across six healthy participants.

Across tasks spanning impulsive perturbations, lunge trajectories, and voluntary limits of stability, GRF-MPC reduced peak planar center-of-mass (CoM) error by 19.6% during perturbations, lowered trajectory tracking error by 24.1%, required 28.7% less net mechanical work, and permitted a 45.9% greater normalized voluntary excursion area.

The underlying QP solves in under 1 ms, comfortably enabling 100 Hz replanning and demonstrating that incorporating live human-ground interaction into predictive control yields stronger, more transparent physical assistance with half the actuators.

summary.en: The paper presents GRF-MPC for upright physical assistance, incorporating live ground reaction force and center-of-pressure measurements into a human centroidal dynamics model. A receding-horizon quadratic program optimizes assistive forces and moments. The method was evaluated on RobUST in an underactuated four-cable setup across nearly 300 trials with six healthy participants, against an eight-cable impedance baseline. The authors report reduced errors and mechanical work, greater voluntary excursion, and sub-millisecond QP solution time across the tested tasks.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向直立式身体辅助的地面反作用力感知模型预测控制（GRF-MPC），将实时地面反作用力和压力中心测量纳入人体质心动力学模型，并通过滚动时域二次规划优化辅助力与力矩。研究在RobUST机器人欠驱动四缆配置上开展近300次试验，涉及6名健康参与者，并与八缆阻抗基线比较。作者报告，在扰动、弓步轨迹和自主稳定性边界任务中，GRF-MPC降低了峰值质心误差和轨迹跟踪误差、减少机械功，并扩大自主运动范围；优化问题求解时间低于1毫秒。

sections.text:
Predicting long action chunks, often spanning dozens of timesteps, has become a key ingredient in increasingly capable robot policies.

In this paper, we find that adapting these long-chunk policies with existing reinforcement learning (RL) methods can require many online samples due to the high dimensionality of the action chunks being optimized, making such adaptation impractical in real-world scenarios where interaction data are costly to collect.

Our key insight is to shift adaptation from optimizing actions to optimizing how long to execute each predicted action chunk. This keeps the adaptation space low-dimensional while its expressivity grows with the chunk size.

We thus introduce Execution at the Right Length (ExRL), a simple approach which augments the base policy with a lightweight adapter that predicts the execution length of each chunk and is trained using off-policy RL algorithms.

Across simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, ExRL enables sample-efficient adaptation of a diverse range of long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

summary.en: The paper argues that online reinforcement-learning adaptation of long-chunk robot policies can be sample-intensive because the action chunks have high dimensionality. ExRL instead adapts the execution duration of each predicted chunk, keeping the adaptation space low-dimensional while retaining expressivity that grows with chunk size. It adds a lightweight adapter to the base policy and trains it with off-policy RL. In simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks, the authors report sample-efficient adaptation across diverse long-chunk policies with minimal task-specific hyperparameter tuning.
summary.zh: 论文指出，使用现有强化学习方法在线适配长动作块策略时，需要优化的动作维度较高，因此可能需要大量样本。ExRL将适配目标从动作本身转为每个预测动作块的执行时长，以保持适配空间较低维，同时使其表达能力随动作块长度增加。该方法为基础策略加入轻量适配器，预测动作块执行长度，并用离策略强化学习训练。作者在仿真基准和真实机器人任务中报告，ExRL可对多种长动作块策略进行样本高效适配，且只需少量任务特定超参数调节。

items.title: ExRL: Sample-Efficient Online Adaptation of Long-Chunk Policies via Execution Length Control

sections.text:
Large-scale demonstration datasets have been central to recent progress in general-purpose robot policies. However, existing datasets are collected in human-absent settings, and policies trained on such data may perform tasks competently in isolation but fail to exhibit human-aware behaviors.

To address this gap, we introduce HABIT, a large-scale robot demonstration dataset for human-present environments.

We organize tasks into three roles capturing distinct modes of human-robot interaction: Collaborator, where human and robot jointly accomplish a task; Coworker, where they pursue separate tasks in a shared space; and Supervisor, where the human directs the robot. The dataset comprises over 10K episodes and over 160 hours across 60 tasks.

Our experiments show that training on human-present data elicits human-aware behaviors that robot-only data fails to produce: spatiotemporal synchronization in Collaborator tasks, yielding in Coworker tasks, and gesture grounding in Supervisor tasks. Moreover, training on HABIT enables rapid adaptation to new human-robot interaction tasks.

By introducing human presence as a new axis of dataset diversity, HABIT extends robot policies to environments shared with humans.

summary.en: The paper introduces HABIT, a large-scale demonstration dataset for robot manipulation in human-present environments. It groups interactions into Collaborator, Coworker, and Supervisor roles and contains over 10,000 episodes, more than 160 hours, and 60 tasks. The authors report that training on this data elicits behaviors not produced by robot-only data: spatiotemporal synchronization, yielding in shared spaces, and grounding human gestures. They also report rapid adaptation to new human-robot interaction tasks.
summary.zh: 论文介绍HABIT，一个面向有人环境的大规模机器人操作演示数据集，涵盖协作、共享空间中各自工作的同事式互动，以及由人类监督指挥三种角色。数据集包含超过1万段情节、160小时和60项任务。作者报告，在该数据上训练能产生仅用机器人数据未能呈现的行为，包括协作任务中的时空同步、同事式任务中的礼让，以及监督任务中的手势理解；训练还支持对新的人机交互任务快速适配。

items.title: HABIT: Human-Aware Behavior and Interaction Training Dataset for Robot Manipulation

sections.text:
In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision.

Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction.

We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

summary.en: The paper studies whether human egocentric videos can support robot policy learning without action supervision. It proposes SPAR, a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture built on a pretrained vision-language model, where future visual-state prediction supplies learning signals complementary to action prediction. The authors report improved performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks from representations learned with egocentric videos, with further gains as video data scales. They also examine objective choices and data curation; the abstract provides no task-specific or quantitative details for these findings.
summary.zh: 本文研究无动作监督的人类第一视角视频如何帮助机器人策略学习。作者提出共享动作与表征预测方法 SPAR：基于预训练视觉语言模型构建 MoT 架构，使未来视觉状态预测与动作预测提供彼此独立且互补的学习信号。作者报告，利用第一视角视频学习的表征可提升分布外机器人任务表现，且视频数据增加时收益进一步提高。研究还考察了目标函数选择和数据整理的影响；这些结论来自文中所述实验，摘要未给出具体任务或量化结果。

sections.text:
Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety.

Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses.

We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior.

This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages.

We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance.

The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues.

Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.

summary.en: The paper presents PA-SaR, a framework coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance around mission-level objectives. It distinguishes environmental ground truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. Single- and multi-robot simulations examine interactions across search-and-rescue stages. Results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion; supervisory allocation improves completion beyond information sharing alone, while more exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, but no improvement in mean or final victim trust or reduction in mortality was detected. Findings are limited to the studied simulation environments.
summary.zh: 本文提出 PA-SaR 框架，协调异构机器人局部控制、学习式探索、监督任务分配和自适应受害者引导，并区分环境真实状态、机器人感知与模拟的受害者行为。作者通过单机器人和多机器人仿真，研究这些机制在搜救任务不同阶段的交互。结果显示，避碰与搜索完成存在权衡；监督分配比单纯信息共享更能提高搜索完成度，而探索增加不必然带来更多救援。相较持续引导，自适应引导增加了救援数，但未检测到受害者平均或最终信任提升，也未发现死亡率下降。结论限于所考察的仿真环境。

sections.text:
Maze navigation requires localization from sparse, repetitive geometry, planning through narrow corridors, and control that stays safe when the estimate or the map is wrong. We present Maze Runner, an open autonomy stack in C++ and ROS 2 that addresses these needs end to end on a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL with a 2D LiDAR in Gazebo.

Perception extracts wall lines from each scan with RANSAC and total least squares, with per-line uncertainty. The same line front end feeds two estimators: an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that localizes against a line map built from the maze mesh, and an EKF SLAM variant that builds the line map online.

Planning runs online on an inflated occupancy grid with A* plus line-of-sight shortcutting, or with a forward-only Hybrid A*.A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) tracks the plan while discrete-time Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) on world-frame LiDAR points keep the robot clear of walls and unmapped obstacles.

The algorithms live in a ROS-free, unit-tested core library, and the whole stack builds and runs from a single reproducible environment.

In simulation, the robot drives a 135 m route through the maze with 1.0 cm localization RMSE against the known map and 24 cm in SLAM mode, the planner returns a path in 6 ms, and the NMPC solves in 11.7 ms on average, never exceeding its 80 ms budget.

summary.en: The paper describes Maze Runner, a C++ and ROS 2 autonomy stack for maze navigation, evaluated in Gazebo with a simulated Husarion ROSbot XL and 2D LiDAR. It extracts wall lines from scans and uses either an extended Kalman filter against a known line map or a SLAM variant that builds the map online. Planning uses A* with line-of-sight shortcuts on an inflated occupancy grid or forward-only Hybrid A*. An NMPC tracks the route, while control barrier functions maintain clearance from walls and unmapped obstacles. In simulation, the robot completed a 135-meter route; reported localization and computation figures apply to this setup.
summary.zh: 本文介绍 Maze Runner，一个用于迷宫自主导航的 C++ 与 ROS 2 系统，在 Gazebo 中的模拟 Husarion ROSbot XL 和二维激光雷达上运行。系统从扫描中提取墙线，并以已知线地图的扩展卡尔曼滤波定位或在线线地图 SLAM 估计位置；规划使用膨胀占据栅格上的 A* 与视线捷径，或仅前进的 Hybrid A*。非线性模型预测控制器跟踪路径，控制障碍函数依据激光雷达点与墙及未建图障碍保持距离。仿真中完成 135 米路线，并报告定位误差、规划耗时及控制器求解时间；这些性能数据属于该模拟设置。

sections.text:
A representation that accurately predicts a deformable object's response is not necessarily the one most useful for choosing manipulation actions. We study this distinction between predictive utility and decision utility in planar single-grasp shape control of Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs).

As a common decision backbone, we introduce Geometry-Pointer-Flow (GPF), a geometry-grounded policy that separates grasp-location selection from grasp-conditioned motion generation.

Its geometry-only variant reduces one-step executed shape error by 32.8% relative to a DLO-specific diffusion policy, while using 18.7 times fewer parameters and achieving approximately 193 times faster inference.

On this backbone, we compare physical context represented by ground-truth parameters, estimated parameters, and learned interaction-history representations, for both forward prediction and executed control.

For prediction, ground-truth physical parameters reduce next-shape error by 15.8% over geometry alone, and estimated parameters are slightly more predictive than interaction history.

This ordering does not carry over to control: estimated parameters provide no detectable one-step control gain, whereas history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF across 470 paired simulation trials.

In closed loop, interaction history improves strict-threshold attainment in simulation and yields the strongest zero-shot performance on hardware. All policies are trained exclusively in simulation and transferred to the physical robot without real-world training or fine-tuning.

These results show that physical context should be evaluated by the decisions it supports rather than by predictive accuracy alone. Code will be released upon acceptance.

summary.en: The paper examines whether representations that predict deformable linear object behavior well also support better single-grasp shape-control decisions, and introduces the geometry-grounded GPF policy. Ground-truth physical parameters improve next-shape prediction, but estimated parameters yield no detectable one-step control gain. In 470 paired simulation trials, history-conditioned GPF reduces executed error by 9.9% relative to geometry-only GPF. sections.text:
Human gameplay supplies paired observations, actions, and visual consequences that can supplement robot-policy training. We study event-and-foresight pretraining for InternVLA-A1.5, combining recorded keyboard/mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision through a frozen video model.

Coverage-preserving anchor selection constructs one-second targets, and an attention mask prevents teacher-forced future actions from entering foresight queries. The selected corpus contains 394 recordings across 20 games, with 223.36 hours of recorded timestamp span and 2,072,084 training anchors.

After 12,400 game-pretraining updates, we compare the resulting initialization with the public base under the same suite-specific robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success increases from 1,718/2,000 (85.90%) to 1,811/2,000 (90.55%), a gain of 4.65 percentage points.

Suite gains are 9.2, 6.8, 0.2, and 2.4 points on Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long. The 40-task breakdown shows 24 improvements, 10 declines, and six ties. These results support the practical value of the complete game-pretraining stage in this evaluated setting, while revealing heterogeneous task outcomes.

The comparison includes additional optimization and does not isolate the effects of game data, the two objectives, or training variability.

It combines keyboard and mouse event prediction with history-conditioned visual supervision, then compares the resulting initialization with a public base model using the same robot fine-tuning protocol. Across four LIBERO suites, aggregate success rises from 85.90% to 90.55%, a 4.65 percentage-point gain. Of 40 tasks, 24 improve, 10 decline, and six tie. The comparison includes extra optimization and does not isolate the contributions of game data, objectives, or training variability.

sections.text:
Task-driven design of soft robots requires the consideration of factors such as geometry, morphology, material properties, and actuation, resulting in a large and complex design space that is challenging to explore. Computational optimisation methods leverage signals from simulation to iteratively improve designs to achieve task objectives.

However, these methods typically demand high computational load for both optimisation and simulation. We present PneuGen, an agentic co-design framework for soft robots that leverages Large Language Model (LLM) agents to search over the soft robot design space efficiently.

A designer agent proposes design programs from a parametric component library, and a separate critic agent analyses simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide reusable physical priors relating geometry and pressure to deformation.

Design programs are automatically validated and converted into finite-element simulations, enabling iterative evaluation.

Across grasping tasks on primitive shapes and challenging objects, as well as shape-matching tasks that require multi-directional planar and 3D deformation, the proposed framework significantly outperforms prior computational optimisation baselines.

Ablation experiments also highlight the utility of the critic agent and the module response model in facilitating efficient design. We additionally demonstrate the agent-generated soft robot designs in real-world shape-matching and grasping tasks.

summary.en: The paper presents PneuGen, a co-design framework that uses large language model agents to search the design space for soft pneumatic robots. A designer proposes programs from a parametric component library, while a critic reviews simulation diagnostics and recommends targeted revisions. Fitted module response models provide physical priors linking geometry and pressure to deformation; programs are validated and converted into finite-element simulations. The authors report that PneuGen significantly outperforms prior computational optimization baselines on grasping and shape-matching tasks. Ablations indicate benefits from the critic and response model, and the paper demonstrates designs on real-world tasks.

sections.text:
Reliable medical laboratory automation requires robots to complete entire workflows in protocol order while handling changes during execution. A robot may execute each motion correctly yet fail the workflow by confusing visually similar stages or stalling after human intervention.

We present Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework that couples explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision--language planner composes an ordered atomic-skill sequence from the protocol and the initial workspace observation.

A multiframe execution monitor detects when the active skill has completed or become infeasible, then advances the workflow or triggers replanning. A skill-conditioned vision--language--action policy generates the manipulation trajectories, and an asynchronous runtime coordinates it with the monitor.

We evaluate Robo-MLT against four policy baselines and a VLM-based monitor baseline on blood gas analysis and blood sample tube sorting, with 50 nominal configurations per method and 20 sample-removal configurations. Robo-MLT achieves task success rates of 82\% and 70\%, exceeding $\pi_{0.5}$ by 30 and 22 percentage points, respectively.

After an operator removes the sample being handled, the system revises the remaining plan and continues processing the other samples. These results indicate that, under the evaluated conditions, explicit workflow monitoring makes long-horizon laboratory manipulation more reliable and recoverable.

summary.en: The paper presents Robo-MLT, a dual-system framework for long-horizon medical laboratory tasks that combines explicit workflow monitoring with learned action generation. A vision-language planner forms an ordered skill sequence; a multiframe monitor detects completion or infeasibility and advances the workflow or triggers replanning, while a skill-conditioned policy generates trajectories. Evaluated on blood gas analysis and tube sorting against policy and monitor baselines, Robo-MLT achieves success rates of 82% and 70%, respectively, exceeding π0.5 by 30 and 22 percentage points. After sample removal, it revises the plan and continues.
summary.zh: 论文提出 Robo-MLT，用于长时程医疗实验室操作的双系统框架，将显式工作流监控与学习式动作生成结合。视觉语言规划器依据流程和初始工作区观测生成有序技能序列；多帧监控器判断技能完成或不可行，并推进流程或触发重规划，技能条件策略生成操作轨迹。作者在血气分析和采血管分拣任务中，将其与四种策略基线及一种监控基线比较；在所测条件下，两项任务成功率分别为82%和70%，高于 π0.5 30和22个百分点。移除正在处理的样本后，系统可修订计划并继续处理其他样本。

sections.text:
Achieving highly dynamic behaviors on humanoid robots, such as running, requires controllers that are both robust and precise, and hence difficult to design.

Classical control theory offers principled tools for stabilizing such systems but struggles to synthesize real-time controllers for their nonlinear, hybrid dynamics; reinforcement learning (RL) handles these dynamics well but typically depends on extensive hand-tuning of heuristic rewards.

In this work, we embed ideas from nonlinear control theory, specifically control Lyapunov functions (CLFs), along with optimized reference trajectories for the hybrid system into the reinforcement learning reward. This approach, CLF-RL, replaces the need to handcraft and tune heuristic reward terms with easy to tune stability informed rewards.

We further develop a trajectory optimization routine that can handle the hybrid structure of the system to produce dynamically feasible, multi-domain, trackable references; using full-order dynamics rather than a kinematic approximation yields up to a 1.7x improvement in position tracking.

The resulting policy runs on a Unitree G1 humanoid with a full flight phase, operating reliably in tight corridors such as a treadmill as well as in outdoor environments, all while remaining robust to disturbances applied to the torso and feet.

Moreover, it achieves accurate global reference tracking utilizing only on-board sensors, making a critical step toward integrating these dynamic motions into a full autonomy stack.

summary.en: The paper presents CLF-RL, which incorporates control Lyapunov functions and optimized reference trajectories for a hybrid system into reinforcement learning rewards, reducing reliance on handcrafted heuristic terms. Its trajectory optimization method accounts for hybrid structure; using full-order dynamics instead of a kinematic approximation yields up to 1.7 times better position tracking. The resulting policy runs on a Unitree G1 with a full flight phase, and the authors report robust operation in corridors and outdoors, disturbance tolerance, and global reference tracking using onboard sensors.
summary.zh: 论文提出 CLF-RL，将控制李雅普诺夫函数和针对混合系统优化的参考轨迹纳入强化学习奖励，以减少手工设计和调节启发式奖励项。作者还提出考虑混合结构的轨迹优化方法；使用全阶动力学而非运动学近似，位置跟踪最高提升 1.7 倍。所得策略在 Unitree G1 人形机器人上运行，包含完整腾空阶段，并在狭窄走廊及室外环境中运行；作者报告其能抵抗躯干和足部扰动，并仅用机载传感器进行全局参考跟踪。

items.title: Chasing Stability: Humanoid Running via Control Lyapunov Function Guided Reinforcement Learning

sections.text:
Pretrained latent world models can support visual planning and control, but their predictions may fail when physical dynamics change at deployment. We study whether such models can adapt from only a few interactions without modifying their pretrained weights or identifying the changed physical parameters.

We introduce a few-shot residual adaptation approach that learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors. The corrections are applied both inside the latent predictor and directly to its predicted latent state, while the pretrained world model remains frozen.

We evaluate the approach in simulation and on a real robot under center-of-mass and friction shifts. These changes reduce the success of the frozen model to near zero. Using three interaction episodes for adaptation, our dual-site approach recovers 90\% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100\% under the modified friction on the real robot.

Ablations show that correcting both locations outperforms single-site adaptation. Our diagnostics further suggest that much of the learned correction reduces a general prediction mismatch, while successful control also depends on shift-specific information captured during adaptation.

summary.en: The paper studies few-shot adaptation of pretrained latent world models when physical dynamics change at deployment. Its residual method learns self-supervised corrections from latent prediction errors without changing pretrained weights or identifying altered parameters, applying corrections both inside the predictor and to its predicted state. In simulation and real-robot evaluations of center-of-mass and friction shifts, the authors report that three interaction episodes recover 90% success under the center-of-mass shift and 100% under modified friction on the real robot. Ablations favor correcting both locations over either one alone.

sections.text:
Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) enable robots to perform manipulation tasks by leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to process visual observations and language instructions.

However, the action prediction objective itself lacks fine-grained task-specific perceptual supervision, making it prone to relying on task-irrelevant visual shortcuts, leading attention away from target objects and key interaction areas, thereby limiting its operational performance and generalization ability.

To address this, we propose Automatic Perception-Guided Attention Alignment for Robot Manipulation ($A^3$-VLA), a framework that derives task-specific visual guidance from the manipulation process itself.

Specifically, $A^3$-VLA first generates heuristic candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, and refines them with a visual segmentation model offline.

These regions serve as explicit perceptual guidance through two complementary objectives: an attention allocation loss that encourages sufficient focus on task-critical regions when language or robot state tokens query the visual input, and a contrastive learning loss that aligns the representations of candidate target regions with language instructions while separating them from task-irrelevant regions.

Extensive experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that $A^3$-VLA consistently improves multiple VLA backbones, with an average success rate gain of 6.5% - 25.2% across benchmarks.

summary.en: The paper introduces A³-VLA, an attention-alignment framework intended to address the lack of fine-grained perceptual supervision in vision-language-action models. It generates candidate regions for target objects and the robot from interaction-induced visual changes, then refines them offline with a segmentation model. An attention allocation loss guides focus toward critical regions, while contrastive learning aligns target-region representations with language instructions and separates irrelevant regions. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks reportedly improve multiple VLA backbones, with average success-rate gains of 6.5% to 25.2% across benchmarks.
summary.zh: 论文提出用于机器人操作的自动感知引导注意力对齐框架 A³-VLA，针对视觉语言动作模型缺少细粒度任务感知监督、可能依赖无关视觉线索的问题。该方法从交互引起的视觉变化中生成目标物体和机器人的候选区域，再离线用视觉分割模型细化；通过注意力分配损失引导模型关注关键区域，并用对比学习使目标区域表征与语言指令对齐、与无关区域区分。作者报告，在模拟和真实操作任务的实验中，该方法提升了多个 VLA 主干模型，基准测试平均成功率增幅为 6.5% 至 25.2%。

sections.text:
System identification requires expert decisions on the identification method, incorporation of prior physical knowledge, and model validation. We propose ASPIRE, a framework for nonlinear system identification in which a large language model agent selects and executes the identification method.

ASPIRE constructs closed-form, nonlinear static or dynamic models from measured data, optionally supplemented by a system description, the intended use of the model, and physical requirements expressed formally or in natural language.

Each model includes its parameters, an estimation record, an interpretation of its terms, and an error evaluated on test data inaccessible to the agent. Formal physical requirements are verified independently. ASPIRE operates autonomously or interactively, allowing the agent to ask questions and the user to request further analyses and identification rounds.

We evaluate ASPIRE on three measured systems: a mobile robot, a rotational system with dry friction, and a laboratory fermenter. Each system is tested with and without a description, in five runs per task. All 30 runs delivered valid models, at a cost of 0.96 to 3.38 US dollars per run.

An assessment by the authors found that, for the 30 models recommended by the agent, one per run, the interpretation of the model and the documentation of its structure selection and parameter estimation fully satisfied 132 of 150 assessed items and partly satisfied 18.

The most frequent discrepancy, found in nine models, concerned inaccurate or unsupported claims about model structure selection.

summary.en: The paper proposes ASPIRE, a nonlinear system-identification framework in which a large language model agent selects and executes identification methods. It builds closed-form static or dynamic models from measurements, optionally using system descriptions, intended use, and physical requirements. Evaluations covered a mobile robot, a dry-friction rotational system, and a laboratory fermenter, with and without descriptions across five runs per task. All 30 runs produced valid models at a reported cost of $0.96 to $3.38 each. The authors also found recurring inaccuracies or unsupported claims about model-structure selection.

sections.text:
We address dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects by presenting SPiD, a physics-informed self-supervised learning framework that couples an accurate deformable object model with an augmented self-supervised training strategy.

On the modeling side, we extend a mass-spring model to more accurately capture object dynamics while remaining lightweight enough for high-throughput rollouts during self-supervised learning. On the learning side, we train a neural controller using a task-oriented cost, enabling end-to-end optimization through interaction with the differentiable object model.

In addition, we propose a self-supervised DAgger variant that detects distribution shift during deployment and performs offline self-correction to further enhance robustness without expert supervision. We evaluate our method primarily on the rope stabilization task, where a robot must bring a swinging rope to rest as quickly and smoothly as possible.

Extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world demonstrate that the proposed controller achieves fast and smooth rope stabilization, generalizing across unseen initial states, rope lengths, masses, non-uniform mass distributions, and external disturbances.

Additionally, we develop an affordable markerless rope perception method and demonstrate that our controller maintains performance with noisy and low-frequency state updates. Furthermore, we demonstrate the generality of the framework by extending it to the rope trajectory tracking task.

Overall, SPiD offers a data-efficient, robust, and physically grounded framework for dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects, featuring strong sim-to-real generalization.

summary.en: The paper presents SPiD, a physics-informed, self-supervised framework for dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects. It combines an extended mass-spring model with task-oriented controller training and offline self-correction for deployment distribution shifts. Simulation and real-world experiments focus mainly on rope stabilization, where the authors report fast, smooth control across unseen initial states, rope properties, and external disturbances. They also describe markerless perception, performance with noisy, low-frequency state updates, and an extension to rope trajectory tracking.
summary.zh: 论文提出 SPiD，一种面向可变形线状物体动态操作的物理信息自监督框架，将扩展的质弹簧模型与任务导向控制器训练结合，并通过检测部署分布偏移进行离线自我修正。在仿真和真实实验中，方法用于绳索稳定任务，表现为快速、平滑，并能适应未见初始状态、绳长、质量分布及外部扰动；作者还报告了无标记绳索感知、低频噪声状态更新下的表现，以及向绳索轨迹跟踪任务的扩展。

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations.

In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies.

Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations.

In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key.

Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.

summary.en: The paper examines how much VLA performance on LIBERO can be explained by retrieving training demonstrations. The authors report 91.7% success without policy training by retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks; under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval has the smallest performance drop among evaluated policies. Analysis of nine public VLAs suggests fine-tuning mainly improves the vision-language backbone as a retrieval key, while actions remain close to demonstrations. The paper also introduces Local Action Consistency, an offline metric reported to track retrieval success and guide retrieval-key training.
summary.zh: 论文考察视觉语言动作模型在 LIBERO 基准上的表现有多少可由训练示范检索解释。作者报告，无需策略训练，仅检索相近示范并复用其动作片段即可达到91.7%的成功率；在 LIBERO-Plus 扰动下，这种检索方法在所评估策略中性能下降最小。对九种公开 VLA 的分析显示，微调主要使视觉语言骨干网络成为更好的检索键，而模型动作仍接近示范。论文还提出离线指标 LAC，用于衡量表示空间中的邻近观测是否对应相似未来动作，并报告该指标可追踪检索成功率、指导检索键训练。

sections.text:
Three-dimensional scene graphs (3DSGs) can provide robots with persistent metric-semantic representations for spatial reasoning, but the existing methods have primarily been developed for indoor and terrestrial environments.

In this paper we investigate how a representative outdoor open-vocabulary method transfers to maritime environments and which adaptations are needed.

Our experiments show that zero-shot representative outdoor 3DSG descriptions agree with our labeled ground truth for a majority of geometry-supported objects on our data, but the resulting map exhibits considerable physical-entity fragmentation, and its terrestrial higher-level assumptions don't capture maritime spatial organization needs.

We therefore keep the underlying mapping method and post-process its accumulated evidence. We show a metric-semantic consolidation method followed by geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language model (VLM) reasoning that reconciles remaining fragments into physical entities and groups entities through observations into local places.

In parallel, we construct maritime macro regions using map priors and onboard water and structure observations, and associate them with the local places.

The resulting representation reduces physical-entity fragmentation beyond both the baseline and our geometry-semantic consolidation component alone, supports correspondence of fixed local places across repeated maritime traversals, and improves contextual retrieval on our reviewed queries over tested baselines.

These results show how an outdoor open-vocabulary map can be adapted into persistent maritime scene memory with our methods for object/place identity and spatial abstractions.

summary.en: The paper investigates adapting an open-vocabulary 3D scene graph method to maritime environments. On the authors’ data, baseline descriptions agree with labeled ground truth for most geometry-supported objects, but the resulting map fragments physical entities and its terrestrial assumptions do not capture maritime spatial organization. The authors retain the mapping method and post-process accumulated evidence through metric-semantic consolidation, geometry-grounded multi-view vision-language reasoning, local-place grouping, and map-prior-based maritime regions. Their experiments report reduced entity fragmentation, correspondence of fixed places across repeated traversals, and better contextual retrieval on reviewed queries than tested baselines.

sections.text:
Embodied Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are backbones for robotic planning and manipulation.

However, for coordinate prediction in grounding tasks, existing architectures suffer from two distinct bottlenecks: discrete tokenization disrupts spatial continuity with high decoding latency, while standard point regression fails on multi-contact affordances and irregularly shaped targets.

To resolve these challenges, we propose PhysMoE, introducing three core contributions: （1） sharing lower layers for multimodal context while routing upper layers to specialized spatial (pixel) and linguistic (text) experts by physical modality, eliminating gradient interference; （2） encoding each coordinate as a single token by reusing the visual encoder's learned positional embeddings, injecting 2D spatial priors to natively align coordinates with visual features and ease training; and （3） differentiable Signed Distance Field (SDF) supervision on pointing, accommodating affordances and irregular geometries without costly mask decoders.

Compared to the base model, PhysMoE achieves a 15.7% average gain and an 8.31x throughput speedup across 9 coordinate-based grounding benchmarks (trajectory, affordance, and localization), while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

summary.en: The paper introduces PhysMoE for coordinate grounding in embodied vision-language models. It shares lower layers for multimodal context, routes upper layers to spatial and language experts, represents each coordinate with one token using learned visual positional embeddings, and applies differentiable signed distance field supervision to pointing. Compared with the base model, the authors report an average gain of 15.7% and an 8.31× throughput speedup across nine coordinate-based grounding benchmarks, while preserving multimodal understanding and reasoning across 11 text-based embodied benchmarks.

sections.text:
Smart industrial solutions that can address multiple tasks require models that understand the underlying processes. We examine representation learning for modeling the injection moulding process as an example of such solutions. We consider its data efficiency and multi-modal benefit compared to classical machine learning alternatives.

To this end, we synthesize a process-informed dataset based on a real reference cycle of an Erlanger Tr\"ager part. We then introduce MouldIt, a temporal convolution and attention based variational autoencoder that reconstructs in-mould signals, while classifying parts as acceptable or as one of our synthetic failure modes.

We evaluate MouldIt on two tasks, known-class classification and unknown-class detection, across nine dataset sizes in single-modal and multi-modal settings. We compare it with an accept-all baseline and the classical methods k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, random forests, and principal component analysis, which we adapt to support both tasks.

MouldIt outperforms classical methods across both tasks from 4000 cycles in the single-modal setting and from 2000 cycles in the multi-modal setting.

It achieves part sorting losses of 6.0 $\pm$ 0.7% and 1.0 $\pm$ 0.3% in the single-modal and multi-modal settings respectively, ranking first across all baselines and a combination of principal component analysis and random forests.

summary.en: The paper studies temporal representation learning for injection moulding and proposes MouldIt, a model combining temporal convolutions, attention, and a variational autoencoder to reconstruct in-mould signals and classify acceptable parts and synthetic failure modes. Using a synthesized dataset based on a real reference cycle, the authors evaluate known-class classification and unknown-class detection across nine dataset sizes and single- and multimodal settings. They report that MouldIt outperforms classical methods from 4,000 cycles in the single-modal setting and 2,000 cycles in the multimodal setting, with lower part-sorting loss in the multimodal setting.
summary.zh: 论文研究注塑过程的时序表征学习，并提出 MouldIt：一种结合时序卷积、注意力与变分自编码器的模型，用于重建模内信号并分类合格部件和合成故障模式。作者基于真实参考周期合成数据集，在九种数据规模及单模态、多模态设置下评估已知类别分类和未知类别检测，并与基线及经典方法比较。摘要报告，单模态数据达到 4000 个周期、多模态达到 2000 个周期后，MouldIt 在两项任务中优于经典方法；其多模态部件分拣损失也低于单模态结果。

sections.text:
We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments.

A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training.

We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency.

An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track.

Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $\pi_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90.

Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

summary.en: The paper presents Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. Its three-stage training uses discrete action-token pre-training, flow-matching mid-training for cross-embodiment control, and real-world post-training. The authors also introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections, alongside a unified end-effector interface, asynchronous action-chunk merging, and event-driven task management. They report 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and fifth place in the RoboDojo VLA track. Comparisons on real-robot tasks and Ethernet insertion are reported under the conditions described in the abstract.
summary.zh: 论文介绍 Meituan-Robotics-0（MR0），一种面向固定底座桌面操作的视觉语言动作模型与具身智能体系统。其训练分为离散动作 token 预训练、基于流匹配的跨本体中期训练和真实世界后训练，并提出将策略替换片段与人工纠正配对的 Rollback 方法。系统还包括统一末端执行器接口、异步动作片段合并及事件驱动任务管理。作者报告 MR0 在 RoboTwin 2.0 的成功率为 93.6%，并在 RoboDojo VLA 赛道排名第五；真实机器人任务比较及以太网插入结果也按摘要所述条件给出。

sections.text:
When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Execution Needs, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation.

Its aligned three-domain track contains 1,080 frozen cases (360 each for coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance).The primary coffee protocols -- closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization -- produce over 115,000 evaluator episodes across evaluated methods, budgets, and inference repeats.

Each case pairs candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, directly measuring whether selected observations support execution. A metadata-assisted diagnostic reference pipeline maintains spatial-functional beliefs and ranks views by missing evidence.

At primary budget settings, it reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; removing functional fields or command binding reduces functional-OOD success to 0.0% and 19.7%, respectively. Under a separate full-preview contract, seven vision-language models reach 26-43%.

Replacing coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores retains 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling these scores reduces success to 15%/11%, supporting dependence on image content. Separately, the aligned three-domain evaluation at H=3 supports portability of the benchmark interface under frozen domain-specific schemas.

These results suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated by whether acquired evidence meets the current command's execution requirements.

summary.en: The paper introduces a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Its frozen cases cover coffee workstations, drawers or cabinets, and appliances, and test whether selected RGB views support commands using hidden postconditions. A metadata-assisted reference pipeline achieves 98.8% closed-loop success and 98.9% functional out-of-distribution success at primary budget settings; removing functional fields or command binding reduces the latter. Separate evaluations examine vision-language models, RGB-derived scores, and portability across the three domains.
summary.zh: 论文提出用于模拟桌面操作的任务条件可行动空间信念基准，包含咖啡工作台、抽屉或柜体、微波炉或家电三个领域的冻结案例，并通过隐藏后置条件评估所选视图是否支持操作执行。元数据辅助参考流程在主要预算设置下达到98.8%的闭环成功率和98.9%的功能性分布外成功率；移除功能字段或命令绑定会降低后者。另有视觉语言模型、RGB视图评分及三领域评估结果，作者据此讨论基准的内容依赖和可移植性。

sections.text:
A humanoid that dances to streamed music must commit each motion chunk before it has heard the music that chunk accompanies, and must continue from motion it has already committed. We present AHEADance, a robot-native streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot by a whole-body tracker.

ListenAhead conditions each chunk on heard music and a frozen music model's forecasts of the coming music, aligned to their target times and weighted by reliability.

The forecasts carry the timing of upcoming beats almost as well as the actual future; with them, the generator is better synchronized with the music and concentrates more motion energy at its song's beat frequency.

Commit Forcing trains continuation from the model's own committed chunks, updating both the latent history and the decoded boundary of the next chunk; it reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%, the level of real dance. Three music evaluators, each validated on real G1 dance, test synchronization, song and style.

On a physical Unitree G1, it dances while the music plays and comes to rest when it stops, without a fall. Project page: https://ihcr.github.io/AHEADance

summary.en: AHEADance is a streaming dance generator executed on a humanoid robot. ListenAhead conditions motion chunks on heard music and forecasts from a frozen music model, aligned to target times and weighted by reliability. The authors report improved synchronization and more motion energy at the song's beat frequency. Commit Forcing trains continuation from already committed chunks and reduces low activity from 83.5% to 10.3%. In a physical Unitree G1 demonstration, the robot dances while music plays and stops when it ends, without falling.

sections.text:
A great gap in adaptivity, flexibility, and dexterity still exists between intelligent robots, whether they are made of rigid or (partially) compliant components, and their naturally evolved animal and vegetal counterparts. One reason could be of `paradigm' nature.

On the one hand, most robots (both rigid and soft) are still designed by following a `Cartesian' approach, with top-down control and a clear mind-body separation. Designing artificial agents on the basis of the principles that we observe in biology is not an easy task.

The principles of organization of animals and plants rely on morphological computation and emergence of fit behaviors from loosely coupled networks of embodied agents. Modeling and control require radically new approaches.

In this paper we briefly recall and explain some seminal mathematical results linking information metrics and dynamics of the agents, already published years ago; we integrate them with some recent methods developed by us and by the community, we highlight some brief remarks about their relevance and we hint to our current and near future work towards finding concrete and efficient ways for the modeling and control of completely or partially compliant artificial agents and for a better understanding of physical intelligence in nature.

We present a technical note summarizing phase-space volume calculations for inverted-pendulum and passive-dynamic walking models, following our proposed framework. Starting from the McGeer compass gait, we introduce knee-ankle compliance, foot-rocker effects, and a Ruina-style compass gait with distributed leg inertia.

Standard heel-strike maps are derived and used in the estimation of viable phase-space volumes $W(\gamma)$, based on a state-dependent Monte-Carlo and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces methods. We show how the methods based on RKHS allow deeper and more subtle analysis.

sections.text:
Navigation in dynamic environments requires mobile robots to make progress toward their goals while respecting motion limits and avoiding surrounding obstacles.

Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem.

This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation.

A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints.

The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty.

Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input.

The selected-policy comparison also shows fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.

items.title: OASIS: Optimization-Aware Subgoal Inference with Safety Constraints for Autonomous Mobile Robot Navigation

sections.text:
Decision making in multi-agent and multi-robot systems often involves discrete decision variables, leading to NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems that must be solved within seconds for near real-time implementation.

Denoising diffusion has emerged as a powerful tool for such problems, but existing approaches face a trade-off: Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) incorporates diffusion in sampling-based optimization (SBO) without training but only over continuous spaces, while existing diffusion-based combinatorial solvers operate over discrete spaces but require offline training.

To this end, we propose Discrete Model-Based Diffusion (Discrete MBD), a training-free SBO method that directly optimizes discrete variables by approximating categorical reverse transition distributions through Monte Carlo sampling.

We establish a finite-step lower bound on the probability of finding a global minimizer and show that this bound converges to one as the number of denoising steps increases.

Extensive experiments on generic integer programs and heterogeneous multi-robot coalition formation and scheduling demonstrate that Discrete MBD outperforms SBO baselines in nearly all settings while achieving solution quality competitive with that of mixed-integer programming and reinforcement learning methods at a fraction of their computational cost.

items.title: Discrete Model-Based Diffusion for Combinatorial Optimization in Multi-Robot Task Allocation

Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process.

We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots.

We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.

sections.text:
Advancing humanoid traversal toward the open world is key to practical deployment in human environments, but remains challenging. The robot must use vision to ensure safe and reliable foot placement on heterogeneous terrain during highly dynamic motion, while producing coordinated, natural whole-body behaviors.

We propose SSR, an efficient end-to-end framework for egocentric vision-based humanoid traversal that jointly learns these capabilities. SSR introduces imagined foothold guidance, which learns to model forthcoming swing-foot contacts and evaluates their support to guide pre-touchdown swings toward stable regions, reducing edge slips.

It further employs equivariant latent-space symmetry augmentation to efficiently induce bilateral coordination under high-dimensional visual observations, and uses terrain-specific multi-discriminator motion priors to encourage human-like behavior across scenes.

Extensive experiments show that SSR achieves safe, stable, and high-quality locomotion on diverse real-world terrains, including stairs with varied structures and extreme challenges such as wide gaps and high platforms, while enabling reliable long-horizon traversal in diverse outdoor environments. Project website: https://ssr-humanoid.github.io/.

sections.text:
In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy.

However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure.

To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations.

Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads.

Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.

items.title: ReACT: Reflection-Consistent Modulation and Cross-Load Consistency for Humanoid Velocity Tracking Under Asymmetric Loads

How can a robot quickly identify and recognize new objects shown to it during a human demonstration? Existing closed-set object detectors frequently fail at this because the objects are out-of-distribution.

While open-set detectors (e.g., VLMs) sometimes succeed, they often require expensive and tedious human-in-the-loop prompt engineering to uniquely recognize novel object instances.

In this paper, we present a self-supervised system that eliminates the need for tedious language descriptions and expensive prompt engineering by training a bespoke object detector on an automatically created dataset, supervised by the human demonstration itself.

In our approach, "Show, Don't Tell," we show the detector the specific objects of interest during the demonstration, rather than telling the detector about these objects via complex language descriptions.

By bypassing language altogether, this paradigm enables us to quickly train bespoke detectors tailored to the relevant objects observed in human task demonstrations. We develop an integrated on-robot system to deploy our "Show, Don't Tell" paradigm of automatic dataset creation and novel object-detection on a real-world robot.

Empirical results demonstrate that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art detection and recognition methods for manipulated objects, leading to improved task completion for the robot.

We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10.

The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$.On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392.

Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations.

A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time.

On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy.

The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes.

We introduce Open-HumanWAM, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanWAM-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language.

Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates.

On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates.

A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers.

We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people.

It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled.

On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.

Foundation models such as GPT and Claude have shown strong capabilities in spatial understanding and embodied intelligence. These advances make agentic robotics a promising path toward artificial general intelligence in robotics.

However, we find that using foundation models to control robots poses serious safety risks, and comprehensive safety evaluation is still lacking. We introduce RoboRisk, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating safety in agentic robotics.

Its 92 simulated tasks and 13 physical-robot tasks fall into five categories: Task-level Refusal (T), Plan Repair (P), Execution-time Hazard (E), Injection (I), and Sequential Memory (S).Prior benchmarks cover at most two of these categories, and several evaluate only text outputs. In contrast, RoboRisk covers all five and executes every task in closed loop.

We evaluate six state-of-the-art foundation models on RoboRisk: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, and Grok 4.7.These models generally show high harm rates. We also evaluate two robot-specific APIs: the Dream API and PokeBot's RoboAPI.

We further propose the Lease-Enforced Agentic Safety Harness (LEASH), which offers essential safety infrastructure for agentic robotics and can be integrated into nearly any agentic architecture.

LEASH leverages a decision model (Jev or OpenAI's Decisions API) to implement task, action, and commit gates, which review the task, each action, and each irreversible operation in their visual context. The planner and all three gates share a common safety policy.

Experiments on RoboRisk in simulation and on physical robots show that LEASH effectively reduces harm across all six foundation models. It largely preserves their task completion performance and adds little time and token overhead.

items.title: LEASH: Stay Safe in Agentic Robotics

Real-robot benchmarks of learned visuomotor policies often record room illuminance as the lighting condition. We show that, on a typical low-cost rig, room light and image light can be almost unrelated.

Four imitation-learning policies (ACT, SmolVLA, Diffusion Policy and pi0.5) were trained on the same 50 demonstrations of a pick-and-place task on an SO-101 arm. Each was run for ten rollouts at about 520 lux and again at about 45 lux, an 11.5x reduction.

Success was 20/40 in normal light and 19/40 in low light: a change of -2.5 percentage points (95% CI -23 to +19), with no evidence that the policies differed in sensitivity (interaction p = 0.86).The recorded video shows why: mean image brightness was only 3% lower in low light on the front camera and 19% lower on the wrist camera.

Both cameras were set to automatic exposure and white balance, which most likely absorbed the difference; exposure was not locked in this experiment. An accidental repeat of one 10-rollout block reproduced its success count (7/10) but matched the first block at only 6 of 10 placements, consistent with chance.

We conclude that lux alone does not describe what a policy sees. Camera settings, and image statistics compared with the training recordings, are the quantities to report and control. Data and code are public.

We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction.

Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally.

LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations.

We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.

Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation.

To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control.

FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing.

It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions.

World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics.

Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video-action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation.

However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot-object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation.

Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture.

Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling.

Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm.

LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.

Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not.

On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other.

When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress.

Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed.

Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.

items.title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
