Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction.

Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks.

We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements.

Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection.

Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.

summary.en: The paper introduces AnchorQ, which uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent action anchors, samples nearby particles, and applies value-guided refinement to improve frozen flow-matching policies. The authors analyze tradeoffs involving identification complexity and support bias, particle refinement and action-class complexity, and the effect of critic accuracy on value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, they report better sample efficiency than post-training baselines. Under the same interaction budget, real-world success rate improved by 37% and simulated task throughput by 97%.

sections.text:
Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code.

We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens.

We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video.

In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03).

Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41.We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.

summary.en: The paper studies whether robot latent action codes can be assigned to reflect the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv). The authors report that independently trained tokenizers assign codes very differently, and that changing inference precision also changes many assignments. They train with a PMv similarity loss alongside video reconstruction. On five held-out shape categories, one run per target yields higher PMv similarity for the PMv-trained tokenizer than released and no-prior tokenizers, but a hand-picked kinematic descriptor scores higher, and a shuffled-label control also scores well. Other targets do not transfer. A downstream test is specified, but its outcome is not reported.

sections.text:
Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter.

An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies.

The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.

summary.en: This paper investigates a controller for a two degree-of-freedom manipulator. An RBF neural network compensator is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space control barrier function filter. An auxiliary state, driven by the difference between requested and applied torque, corrects the learning signal to reduce the filter’s direct effect on adaptation. The authors evaluate a two-link manipulator using constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. They report improved tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, with contributions from both shared compensation and auxiliary correction.

sections.text:
Enabling robots to infer interaction-relevant physical properties from vision before contact would improve planning and control in unstructured environments. Vision provides useful pre-contact information, but appearance alone is often ambiguous: visually similar regions can induce different friction, stiffness, or sinkage responses upon contact.

Existing approaches often collapse this ambiguity to a point estimate or aggregate experience through fixed semantic classes, limiting their ability to preserve distinct physical regimes.

Instead, we propose a real-time estimator that replaces semantic class indexing with an interaction-grounded Gaussian-mixture posterior over latent physical parameters, conditioned directly on continuous visual embeddings.

Our approach maintains interaction-derived Gaussian parameter estimates, typically from inverse modeling, as mixture components while using embedding similarity to retrieve and weight relevant past interactions for each new query region.

A support-aware fusion mechanism incorporates a conditional generative prior model when interaction history is sparse, while a learned embedding refinement improves retrieval relevance without discretizing the representation.

Our experiments show that the estimator recovers multimodal physical beliefs, rejects unrelated interaction history, avoids spatial map discretization, and evaluates at controller rates.

In a high-fidelity autonomous racing simulation with unknown low- and high-friction surface regions, the posterior enables the controller to adapt over repeated laps as interaction evidence accumulates, improving performance while maintaining friction-aware behavior.

summary.en: The paper proposes a real-time estimator that uses continuous visual embeddings to retrieve and weight relevant past interactions, representing interaction-derived Gaussian parameter estimates as mixture components in a multimodal posterior over latent physical properties. When history is sparse, support-aware fusion adds a conditional generative prior, and learned embedding refinement improves retrieval. The authors report that experiments recover multimodal beliefs, reject unrelated interactions, and run at controller rates. In a high-fidelity autonomous racing simulation, the controller adapts over repeated laps as evidence accumulates while maintaining friction-aware behavior.

sections.text:
While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure.

We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface.

PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees.

The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface.

Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering.

At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS.

summary.en: The paper introduces PLS-GS, which uses camera and high-definition LiDAR data to build a compact 3D Gaussian Splatting representation aligned with measured surfaces. It jointly fits a hierarchical Gaussian mixture over position and color, then uses its components to constrain renderable Gaussians in local surface frames, with a Mahalanobis support loss limiting deviation from LiDAR-derived surfaces. Across five large outdoor scenes, the authors report closer placement to LiDAR measurements with substantially fewer primitives and faster rendering. At matched capacity, rendering quality is comparable.

sections.text:
The motion of an articulated part in cluttered surroundings is constrained not only by an object's intrinsic joint limits but also by extrinsic obstacles. However, existing approaches primarily consider object articulation properties alone.

Here we present Motion Constraint Prediction Network (MoCo-Net), a two-stream neural network that jointly predicts the continuous motion ranges of articulated parts and obstacle heatmaps highlighting potential collision regions from partial-view point cloud observation.

By capturing both internal and external motion constraints, MoCo-Net produces more accurate feasible motion range prediction and obstacles recognition, improves generalization for novel objects in new scenes, and enables robots to construct a scene configuration space for efficient exploration of rearrangement actions.

Our experiments show that MoCo-Net's two-stream design enhances each other to deliver more accurate predictions, which subsequently form a compact configuration space for a customized planner to efficiently rearrange the scene.

summary.en: The paper presents MoCo-Net, a two-stream neural network that predicts continuous motion ranges of articulated parts and heatmaps of potential collision regions from partial-view point clouds. It models both intrinsic joint limits and external obstacle constraints, aiming to improve feasible motion and obstacle predictions and help robots build a scene configuration space for exploring rearrangement actions. The authors report that experiments show the two streams enhance one another’s prediction accuracy, producing a compact configuration space that a customized planner uses to rearrange scenes efficiently.
